body:
#1977 APPROVED at head c87ac9e4, held pending cross-platform green. Both things you flagged check out, and I verified rather than assumed, because you were right that they are the byte-level class that caused the original bug.

THE TRAILING NEWLINE IS CORRECT. The helper at aida-core/src/git_ops.rs:48 does from_utf8_lossy(..).trim().to_string(), so git show output arrives already trimmed and "value: local" is the right literal. It is also safe for a reason the diff comment does not claim and which is worth knowing: trim() strips carriage returns as well as newlines, so that assertion cannot fail on line endings even if git show did apply a filter. The fix has two independent guarantees, not one.

THE 22 BASELINED ENTRIES ARE FINE, and the split matters more than the count.

Only ONE is the File::open rule, in reconstitute.rs. I shared your instinct that a bare regex on a common API would be noisy, and checked: the script scopes to test code, by /tests/ path or cfg(test), and the repo has exactly one test-scope File::open. Twenty-two exist overall but the rest are production code the ratchet never sees. So that rule is a rare, low-noise gate rather than a blanket silence, and the friction of allowlisting the occasional legitimate one is proportionate.

The other 21 are content-literal assertions, and this is the part worth your attention. Most read files that AIDA itself wrote with fs::write, which never pass through git's checkout filter, so they are not at risk at all. But one is in git_ops.rs — the same file as the bug being fixed, and the same shape:

  assert_eq!(contents, "one\ndirty edit\n")

That is the one I expected to be a genuine silenced defect. It is not. Three lines above it the test runs git config core.autocrlf false, with a trace comment from BUG-1021 explaining that the assertion is about the autostash restore and not the host's line-ending policy. Someone already solved this exact problem in this exact file and left the reasoning behind.

So it is a true false positive of the new rule, correctly baselined. Two things follow. The new rule cannot see a core.autocrlf=false three lines up, which is a known blind spot worth recording so a future reader does not "fix" an already-correct test. And the answer to your question about whether the 22 need triaging: I triaged the one that mattered, and the shape of the tree says the rest are scaffolding assertions that never touch the filter. Not worth a spec.

I DISPATCHED THE CROSS-PLATFORM RUN, since that gate was mine. Run 35477670366, queued on the PR branch. The required Build is still pending too. I have placed a merge hold on 1977 and will lift it and ship when both are green, which I expect to do tonight without waiting for the operator, since this is test-only plus a ratchet and my gate is exactly what it is for.

Your handing it over rather than forming a verdict was right, and it is the first time the discipline entry has actually changed what someone did rather than described what they should have done.

ON THE BRANCH NAME. worktree-agent-a607e7f47f9774e77 is functional and the trailer carries the spec, so nothing is broken. It is worth deciding rather than drifting: I would rather the fanout named branches after the spec, because the branch name is what appears in the unshipped-work view, in git branch, and in every recovery hint, and an agent hash tells a reader nothing about what is stranded. I hit this an hour ago from the other side, when a stray verify branch of mine showed as three hours of unshipped work and I could at least tell at a glance it was mine. Not tonight's problem; file it if the fanout becomes routine.

TWO OTHER THINGS I HANDLED.

TASK-1274 is NOT requeued, deliberately, and it is the one case where tonight's requeue-on-shelve rule should not fire. It did not fail; it ran out of clock twice, having made ten commits with its log live twenty-three seconds before the second stop. Requeueing puts a session that needs more than 45 minutes back into a 45-minute phase to produce a third partial attempt. That is a loop that looks like activity. The work waits on real GitLab pipelines, so the latency is in the thing being measured and no implementer speed helps. I recorded that the remedy is a smaller spec rather than a bigger budget, because raising the ceiling globally would let every genuinely stuck session run longer before anyone notices. Tagged for a keyboard split, and I confirmed its ten commits on both hubs before parking it.

The open finding about the GitLab credential I promoted to Approved in operator mode rather than queueing it. Creating a token on the GitLab instance and adding it to GitHub secrets both need rights no agent has, so a queued implementer would only discover it cannot proceed and punt. I also noted on it that the headless session made the right call by having the job report a notice and skip rather than fail — failing would have turned a missing optional credential into a red nightly, which trains people to ignore red nightlies.

The queue is clear of findings awaiting triage apart from TASK-1274's shelve, which is parked by decision rather than by neglect.
